extracted.intended_audience: novelists, writers of long fiction, and students of literary technique/criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on methods of fiction—contrast between panoramic/pictorial and scenic/dramatic treatment of a story, with rules for when to use each, how to handle narrator authority, detail, time, and climactic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic vs scenic presentation (picture and drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental distinction of method: the 'panoramic' or 'pictorial' presentation (a broad survey, the author surveying a landscape of life) contrasted with the 'scenic' or dramatic presentation (action shown directly, as enacted before the reader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the panoramic/pictorial method when you wish to give a general impression of a world or a large sweep of life (example: Thackeray's Vanity Fair). Use the scenic/dramatic method when immediacy and enacted detail are required (example: Maupassant). The two are not sharply separable but the choice should suit the story's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity by typicity and impression rather than intricate plot
rubrics_metrics.description: For panoramic works the unity of the book often 'depends in truth upon one fact only'—that the crowd of characters are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world depicted, so the book is the story they unite to tell rather than the tightly woven plot of any single individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building a novel as an impression of a time or society, prioritize creating representative, typical figures and a coherent social atmosphere over forcing an intricate plot connection between every character. Example: Vanity Fair's unity comes from its portrait of a social world rather than a single central plotline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make functional rather than merely decorative panoramas
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic or descriptive chapters must be 'functional'—serving as a hinge or contributing to the course of a character's career—rather than decorative patches that do not advance meaning or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure impressionistic or summary passages have a clear role (e.g., marking a turning point, preparing a climax). The Curzon Street chapters in Vanity Fair are praised because they form the hinge of Becky's career; theatrical or picturesque episodes that do not serve the book's purpose feel wasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a climax demands drama, show it (do not merely summarize)
rubrics_metrics.description: If material converges on a decisive question (e.g., 'Does Becky fail in the end?'), the most convincing answer is the immediate, enacted scene—not a retrospective account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place climactic events 'immediately before us' in present action to secure their force; avoid relying on authorial summary for the concluding revelation. Failure to do so may force theatrical or crude devices to compensate for lack of direct enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare dramatic scenes adequately to avoid artificial theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic handling frequently neglects advance preparation for a full dramatic scene; without preparation the scene, when finally enacted, can look 'artificial' or 'theatrical' because characters are not readied to act independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene will be performed directly, plant sufficient characterization, prior enactments, or structural support so the characters can 'take the matter into their own hands' plausibly; otherwise the scene may feel forced or crude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of detail: hint, moment, glance
rubrics_metrics.description: In panoramic narration brief hints, moments, and glances often suffice to illustrate and enrich the general picture; incidents arise 'by the way' and serve as illustrative flashes rather than full scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective, telling details rather than continuous particularization. Short illustrative incidents (a look, a remark, a brief tableau) can enrich a broad panorama without interrupting the overall flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening and subordination of instance to broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic/pictorial art involves the foreshortening and generalizing of particular instances so that single occasions are subordinated to a broader impression or tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a pictorial effect, subordinate specific events to the cumulative impression; let episodes appear as illustrative fragments that feed the general sensation of place and life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate the narrator's authority ('dramatize the seeing eye')
rubrics_metrics.description: The panoramic method tends to make the author's mind visible (the omniscient narrator). To avoid an unaccountable narrator and loose ends, the novelist should make the point of view accountable within the book—'dramatize the seeing eye.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include devices that make the narrator's perspective part of the fictional world (signals, framed voice, verifiable vantage points) or else avoid overusing an intrusive omniscient voice. Without such authentication, the reader may be drawn away from the fiction into questions about the narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend authorial vision with a character's perspective to mask the narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to avoid an intrusive authorial presence is to blend the author's acuter vision with a character's own perception so that the narrative voice seems to arise from within the story rather than external to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert's technique of blending his vision with Emma's experience is cited: the author's observations are merged with the character's, reducing overt authorial intrusions. Use this to preserve pictorial sweep without exposing an unverified omniscient eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate chronology and focus to convey time as stored/tranquil
rubrics_metrics.description: Time can be handled not as movement but as 'tranquillity'—layers of time stored in description by leisurely play with chronology and shifting focal distance (example: Castlewood in Esmond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create 'time-pictures' let chronology breathe: delay, return, shift focus between near and far, and accumulate details that give the sensation of time deepening rather than simply passing. This is a deliberate technique for impression rather than sequential action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict variety of method to the work's 'bare needs' and use resources scrupulously
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel may exhibit a variety of methods, but these should be carefully restricted to what the story requires and resources must be used scrupulously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous stylistic shifts; let diversity of method serve the work's needs rather than distract. Madame Bovary is recommended as an example of 'variety of method, and with its careful restriction of that variety to its bare needs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wasting potentially dramatic material as mere picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Large occasions that naturally call for dramatic treatment (e.g., a ball, a historic revelry) can be dissipated into mere picture if handled panormically, resulting in lost effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when an episode is inherently dramatic and resist converting it into a decorative panorama. The Waterloo ball in Vanity Fair is cited as a misspent dramatic opportunity—do not let important events leave no image or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the author's personal relation to the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors cultivate a 'talkative, confidential' relation with the reader (Thackeray), while others strive for anonymity; the choice affects method and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a strongly personal narrator can enrich a panoramic chronicle but also risks drawing attention away from the fictional world. If the narrator is personal, either commit to that mode or take steps to balance it so the book remains internally complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make narrative incidents illustrate rather than dominate the general tone
rubrics_metrics.description: In pictorial narration incidents should 'illustrate what he has to say'—they arise to exemplify the larger impression and then the stream proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let episodes serve as illustrative highlights that enrich the overall mood; avoid letting episodic incident overpower the intended general effect when the aim is pictorial rather than strictly dramatic.
